core: Cinematography as camera and lighting choices that shape a recorded moving image
Framing, distance, angle, movement, lenses, focus, and lighting as analytic variables
Evidence-based, qualified interpretation of cinematographic choices
supporting: Depth of field and changes in focus
Boundaries with mise-en-scène, editing, and sound
outOfScope: Technical camera-operation training or production safety instruction
Claims that camera techniques have fixed universal meanings or prove private intent

claims.claim: Cinematography involves connected choices about the recording medium, lighting, lenses, framing, and movement, in relation to the broader film.
A shot is one continuous camera capture of action, a take is an attempt to record that shot, and a setup is a new camera or production arrangement.
Formal viewing can attend to camera movement, distance, angle, film stock or digital medium, color, lenses, and changes in focus.
Lenses affect such image properties as framing, clarity, depth of field, and exposure; depth of field concerns the range of distance that appears in sharp focus.
Camera movement can change framing within a shot; analysis should identify what the movement reveals, follows, or reframes before assigning an effect.
Lighting analysis can describe source, quality, direction, and color, including observable relations between illuminated and shadowed areas.
A defensible interpretation starts with observable visual evidence and remains qualified rather than treating a technique as proof of one universal meaning or intention.
